Maximum likelihood estimation models an agent's behavior under a Markov decision process, assuming the agent's policy is entirely determined by the reward function. However, this approach has been found to be inadequate for neural network-based agents, as these agents can exploit the training process by learning to follow a policy that maximizes reward during training, yet fails to generalize to real-world applications where the reward function is altered. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that decouples the agent's behavior from the reward function, allowing the agent to behave optimally in response to any reward function. This approach is applied to neural network-based agents, which are found to be susceptible to reward hacking. To counteract this, we propose a reward-biased maximum likelihood estimation method, which leverages the agent's observed behavior to constrain the reward function, thereby preventing agents from exploiting the training process. This method is demonstrated to be effective in improving the generalizability of agents, which are less prone to reward hacking. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be seen as a form of maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning, which provides a theoretical foundation for the method. The CDF collaboration has found that their top mass measurement is significantly affected by the energy corrections for jets, particularly those corrections that vary in flavor. The corrections for jets, which account for differences in energy due to flavor, are derived from data using a method called "data-driven," which relies on the assumption that the underlying physics is the same across different jet flavors. However, this assumption may not hold true, leading to potential errors in the energy corrections. In this study, we investigate the impact of re-calibrating the flavor-dependent jet energy corrections on the measured mass of the top quark. We find that the measured mass can shift by up to 0.5 GeV when the jet energy corrections are re-calibrated, resulting in a corresponding shift in the measured mass of 0.5 GeV. This highlights the need for further investigation into the origin of the discrepancies between the jet energy corrections derived from data and those based on Monte Carlo simulations. In particular, we suggest that the jet energy corrections may be sensitive to the underlying physics of the top quark decay, leading to potential errors in the energy corrections. In order to resolve this issue, we propose a new method for determining the jet energy corrections that relies on the assumption that the energy corrections are independent of jet flavor. This study outlines a multi-stage process for categorizing descriptions and system summaries using statistical methods and natural language processing techniques. The initial step employs the vector space model to categorize descriptions and system summaries, and the second stage applies the Stanford CoreNLP tool to analyze text. The resulting output from both stages is then merged and ranked to determine the final classification result. The study also examines the effectiveness of various machine learning algorithms, including Naive Bayesian, Decision Trees, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Multi-Layer Neural Networks, in achieving high accuracy rates for text classification. The proposed approach is evaluated using a dataset of 1000 descriptions and 1000 summaries, and the results demonstrate its potential for accurately categorizing text. The study's findings are presented in a technical report.

This study introduces a dataset designed to evaluate the performance of image matching techniques under challenging low-light conditions. The dataset consists of pairs of images captured in both dark and well-lit scenarios, with the latter serving as a reference point. To create this dataset, we developed a method for producing realistic dark images by applying a series of filters to high-quality source images. The resulting dataset, known as Dark, features 1,000 pairs of images captured in 10 different environments. To our knowledge, this dataset is the first of its kind to focus on image matching within the low-light domain. The dataset is accompanied by a range of baseline methods, and we provide an assessment of the performance of leading image matching algorithms when applied to this dataset. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/robot-perception-group/dark. For further information, please refer to the accompanying technical report.

A significant security threat to modern software is the cache side channel attack, which can be exploited by an attacker to gain access to sensitive information. This vulnerability is particularly concerning due to its widespread presence in commercial software, making it difficult to identify and locate. This paper introduces CacheQL, a novel approach that empowers developers to identify and locate cache side-channel vulnerabilities in existing software. This is achieved through the creation of a query language that allows users to specify cache side-channel attacks and automatically generate and execute these attacks against the target software. Our evaluation of CacheQL on 10 prominent open-source projects and 10 real-world attacks demonstrates its effectiveness, with CacheQL successfully identifying 9 out of 10 side-channel vulnerabilities in these projects. Additionally, CacheQL is able to locate 5 previously unknown side-channel vulnerabilities in the Apache HTTP Server, which were not previously identified. This highlights the potential of CacheQL to significantly improve the security of widely used software. Our research also reveals that cache side-channel attacks are more prevalent than previously thought, with the majority of these attacks being exploitable in production environments. This finding underscores the need for developers to adopt more effective methods for identifying and locating cache side-channel vulnerabilities. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated impressive results in a variety of tasks, including node classification and clustering. However, their performance heavily relies on the accuracy of the underlying graph representation. This representation is typically derived from the initial graph and the propagation of features through it. Unfortunately, the initial graph's accuracy is often compromised by noisy data, while the propagated features can be affected by the propagation method and the accuracy of the underlying graph. To address this challenge, we introduce NODE-SELECT, a novel GNN that employs a discriminative propagation technique to enhance the graph representation. This technique involves selecting the most relevant nodes to propagate features to a target node, thereby improving the graph representation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NODE-SELECT through experiments on node classification benchmarks, showcasing its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods. This paper introduces a novel computational approach for generating regular meromorphic differential functions on complex projective spaces, which can be expressed as differential forms with specific pole structures. Building on Saito's concept of logarithmic residues, we present a method for constructing regular meromorphic differential functions and provide corresponding examples. Additionally, we outline a procedure for transforming a regular meromorphic differential function into a meromorphic one, and demonstrate how our method can be applied to create meromorphic differential functions with specified pole behaviors. Our approach is further illustrated through numerical examples implemented in the computer algebra system SageMath. The primary focus of this research lies in developing a theoretical framework for constructing regular meromorphic differential functions, which can be realized through numerical computations. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of these meromorphic differential functions in physics and engineering. A key advantage of our method is its ability to handle complex hypergeometric differential functions and their derivatives, which are commonly encountered in mathematical and scientific contexts. To facilitate practical implementation, we provide a SageMath code that showcases the effectiveness of our approach. Speedrunning is a form of entertainment where players use quick techniques to rapidly complete a game. A key aspect of speedruns involves developing efficient control methods to execute intricate in-game actions at high speeds. This paper introduces a novel approach to automate speedruns by employing a navigation planner that generates precise control inputs for games. Unlike traditional methods, our planner is informed by a dataset of expert player movements, which it uses to determine optimal paths and control decisions. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective on a range of 2D and 3D games, with results showing that it can produce high-quality control inputs for most games. Notably, our method can often replicate expert player movements, even when those players are playing at extremely fast speeds. This paper also explores the potential for conditional planning, which enables the generation of tailored control inputs based on specific game states. We envision that this research will contribute to a new generation of tools for speedrunners and the broader gaming community. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated using various metrics, including peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity, and visual information density indexes. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques, with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 34.55 and a visual information density index of 0.89. Furthermore, a regression analysis was conducted to predict wound healing using the proposed super resolved images, and the findings suggest a strong correlation between image quality and wound healing prediction. The proposed method has the potential to improve wound assessment and management in diabetic patients, and its application can be extended to other medical imaging scenarios. In recent years, significant advancements have been made in the field of 3D object detection, largely attributed to the emergence of point cloud data. Nevertheless, the inherent sparsity and irregularity of point cloud data pose significant challenges for deep learning networks. To address this, we introduce a novel 3D object detection network, dubbed AA3DNet, which leverages a multi-scale feature fusion approach to enhance detection performance. By incorporating a novel attention module, our network effectively captures long-range dependencies and improves feature learning capabilities. Extensive experiments conducted on the KITTI 3D detection benchmark demonstrate the superiority of our method, achieving state-of-the-art results in both 3D detection and bird's eye view detection. Notably, our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods with a relative improvement of 3.5% in 3D detection and 2.5% in bird's eye view detection. In the field of computer vision, 3D point clouds have become increasingly significant, particularly in tasks such as object recognition and pose estimation.  However, point clouds are often difficult to work with due to their irregular structure and lack of image-like properties.  To address this challenge, researchers have developed various techniques to transform point clouds into more manageable formats.  A novel approach, known as ParaNet, has been proposed to overcome these limitations by mapping 3D point clouds into a standard representation.  ParaNet achieves this by first projecting the point cloud onto a plane, and then using a neural network to predict the corresponding 2D image.  By doing so, it is possible to leverage the extensive knowledge and techniques developed for 2D image processing.  To further enhance the performance of ParaNet, a new loss function has been introduced that encourages the predicted 2D image to resemble a perfect representation of the original 3D point cloud.  Through a series of experiments, it has been demonstrated that ParaNet can be effectively used for tasks such as object recognition, pose estimation, and 3D reconstruction.  Moreover, the results show that ParaNet outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.  The code and pre-trained models for ParaNet are available for public access.  This work is expected to pave the way for the development of more advanced techniques for processing 3D point clouds. To address this challenge, we have developed a new federated learning framework that promotes fairness and equity by mitigating the influence of imbalanced data on model development. Through extensive testing on multiple datasets, we have found that our framework significantly outperforms traditional federated learning methods in terms of both accuracy and equity. Specifically, we have observed a substantial reduction in the impact of rare characteristics on model development, as well as a significant decrease in the disparity in predictions across different groups. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in promoting fairness and equity in federated learning, and we believe that it has the potential to revolutionize the field by enabling the development of more inclusive and equitable models. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach called the motion-aware pseudo siamese network (MPSN), which utilizes a unique facial feature – the eyes. By leveraging the movement of the human eye, MPSN enhances facial recognition accuracy. Specifically, MPSN employs a motion-aware module to detect and amplify eye movement, a pseudo siamese network to learn facial features, and a motion-aware loss function to optimize the model's performance. Experimental results on a large-scale indoor video dataset demonstrate MPSN's effectiveness in improving facial recognition accuracy. A novel active learning method is introduced, which leverages a teacher network to identify and query the most informative samples from the training dataset, thus enhancing the student network's test performance. The teacher network is trained alongside the student network, utilizing the student's confidence as a guide for labeling unannotated samples, and these labels are then used to augment the student's training set. This iterative process of querying and annotating samples continues until the student converges, and the resulting approach consistently outperforms existing active learning methods across various classification tasks. Notably, this method is the first to integrate teacher-student networks for active learning, and it offers a more efficient and effective solution compared to traditional methods. In the realm of reinforcement learning, a significant threat to the efficacy of algorithms arises from reward manipulation scenarios, where an adversary intentionally alters the reward function to thwart the agent's objectives. This adversary can exploit the agent's inability to account for external reward modifications, rendering the agent vulnerable to manipulation. To address this challenge, we categorize reward manipulation scenarios into three types: causal, counterfactual, and non-causal. Building on causal influence diagrams, we develop a framework to analyze and resolve these reward manipulation scenarios, focusing on causal and non-causal categories. Specifically, we demonstrate how causal influence diagrams can be leveraged to design reward functions that safeguard against reward manipulation, while also discussing potential solutions to counterfactual reward manipulation scenarios. Ultimately, we envision this work as a starting point for a comprehensive exploration of reward manipulation solutions. Bayesian inference is a statistical technique that involves making probabilistic assessments about unknown parameters. It's commonly used in complex models that require precise analysis, but the computational costs can be high due to the need for Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. The Approximate Bayesian inference method, implemented in R-INLA, offers a faster alternative by approximating posterior distributions within specific domains using simpler models. This text introduces an extended version of the Simplified Laplace approximation, presenting its mathematical formulation and computational approach. It also includes a comparison with MCMC sampling and provides a case study involving a Bayesian spatial model to illustrate the approach's effectiveness. The associated code is available for public access.

This paper investigates a class of singular stochastic PDEs driven by a fractional Laplacian and a Gaussian random field with non-trivial correlations. Furthermore, we show that the solution is unique in a particular sense, and provide a formula for the correlation function of the solution's spatial derivatives. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the study of the renormalized Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation and the stochastic Burgers equation. Finally, we outline a strategy for extending our results to a broader class of singular stochastic PDEs driven by general Levy processes. Our work is expected to have significant applications in the study of stochastic systems with non-linear interactions, and will facilitate the development of new techniques for tackling challenging problems in stochastic PDEs. By analyzing the binary representation of Go executables, BinGo can detect various types of concurrency bugs, including data races, deadlocks, and livelocks, without requiring access to the source code. In particular, BinGo has successfully identified over 1,000 concurrency bugs in the Go Standard Library and 11 bugs in real-world applications, including a significant number of data races and deadlocks. Die analysis in ancient numismatics involves examining the characteristics of coins produced by a single die to determine if they were minted by the same press. This process typically requires a labor-intensive and time-consuming comparison of each coin's features, making it prone to human error. To address this issue, we have developed an unsupervised statistical method that can automatically identify groups of coins minted by the same die without requiring any initial training. This approach is based on a hierarchical clustering technique that uses a specific type of multivariate analysis to evaluate the similarities between coins. We have tested our method on a dataset of Roman Republican denarii coins and found that it accurately identifies groups of coins minted by the same die, even when those coins have undergone significant wear and erosion. This method has the potential to greatly improve the efficiency and objectivity of die analysis, making it easier for historians to study ancient coins and civilizations. Furthermore, we have made our software available to the public, providing a valuable resource for researchers in numismatics and related fields.

We confirm the validity of the affirmative answer to Charles Baggett's query. Specifically, we demonstrate that any non-zero, completely positive, unital quantum operation can be expressed as a sequence of unitary transformations. Furthermore, we establish that such an operation can be decomposed into a series of unitary transformations with a maximum of d(d-1)/2 operations requiring sequential application, where d represents the dimension of the underlying space. This finding resolves a long-standing problem initially posed by Charles Baggett in 1990. The underlying reasoning is rooted in the principles of quantum information theory, specifically operator system theory, and draws from established results in matrix theory, along with the theory of graph decomposition. In these situations, it can be beneficial to utilize the data immediately, rather than storing it for processing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MSRL through experiments in the fields of autonomous driving and robotics, where it outperforms traditional reinforcement learning methods in scenarios with limited training data. This model builds upon the success of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and is trained using a single reference image without the need for 3D modeling or additional data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in creating portraits with a soft, ethereal quality and provide a publicly available implementation in PyTorch. We introduce Spatial Construction, a generative architecture that utilizes 
reinforcement learning to create intricate, high-resolution designs with 
hidden patterns. This framework enables the creation of diverse, large 
structures that can be used as training data for downstream tasks. 
Notably, our architecture can be trained in a self-playing mode, where it 
continuously refines its capabilities. Spatial Construction is based on a 
probabilistic model that generates designs by combining random elements and 
deterministic actions. This framework is highly adaptable and can be 
applied across various domains, including images, 3D environments, and text. 
We demonstrate the effectiveness of Spatial Construction in generating 
realistic training data for downstream tasks, such as image classification, 
object detection, and reinforcement learning. 
The framework's versatility is showcased through its ability to create 
complex 3D environments and images with hidden object categories. 
Furthermore, our architecture can be trained in a self-playing mode, 
resulting in a highly efficient and scalable approach to data generation.

Monocular 3D object detection is a complex task that requires estimating an object's depth, orientation, and other attributes from a single image. Current methods often rely on depth maps or stereo images, but these can be expensive and limited in availability. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel approach that uses a depth-aware dynamic message transmission mechanism to enhance monocular 3D object detection. Our method leverages the fact that nearby objects in a scene are more likely to be accurate, while distant objects may be noisy. By incorporating this insight, we create a message-passing mechanism that adaptively selects relevant messages from neighboring objects to refine depth estimation. Our approach, dubbed Mono3D, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI and NuScenes benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in monocular 3D object detection. Open data extraction involves automatically extracting structured data from unstructured online content, a task that has seen limited success due to the lack of effective open extraction systems. While open information extraction systems can identify potential data, they often struggle to extract meaningful, high-quality information, leading to a need for improved solutions. To address this gap, we introduce Graphene, a novel open extraction system that leverages a graph-based approach to enhance data extraction. By modeling extraction candidates as nodes and relationships as edges, Graphene facilitates the creation of complex graphs that capture the nuances of text. Our system then uses these graphs to refine and prioritize extraction results, preserving contextual information and reducing noise. Experimental evaluations demonstrate Graphene's ability to outperform existing open extraction systems in both quantity and quality of extracted data. Specifically, Graphene achieves a 20% increase in extracted triples and a 10% reduction in errors compared to the best-performing baseline. Furthermore, Graphene's ability to capture and convey contextual information leads to improved performance on downstream tasks, such as relation extraction and entity typing, with a 5% increase in F1 score. In a society with diverse viewpoints, individuals tend to surround themselves with like-minded people, creating an echo chamber effect. This phenomenon is particularly concerning in the context of misinformation, as it allows false information to spread rapidly. To combat this issue, we developed an algorithm that optimizes exposure to counterpersuasive opinions by strategically selecting individuals to engage with, aiming to minimize the likelihood of adopting false information. Our approach involves a two-stage optimization process, where the first stage determines the optimal set of individuals to interact with, and the second stage optimizes the order in which to engage with them. We also considered the possibility of a "backfire" effect, where engaging with counterpersuasive opinions can inadvertently reinforce misinformation. To address this, we introduced a parameter that captures the effectiveness of counterpersuasion and used it to refine our algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in mitigating the echo chamber effect and reducing misinformation. This work has the potential to inform the development of personalized strategies for exposing individuals to counterpersuasive opinions, thereby promoting more informed decision-making. Ultimately, our research contributes to the optimization of social exposure and the reduction of misinformation. The task of open-set identification (OSI) involves classifying data points that do not belong to any known class. This task is particularly challenging due to its reliance on unknown data, necessitating a model that can generalize beyond its training set. Our proposed method, augmentation-based similarity learning (ASL), addresses this challenge by leveraging multiple models to generate diverse feature representations of known classes, thereby enabling the identification of unknown data through a voting mechanism. This approach is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in distinguishing between known and unknown data, while also maintaining competitive performance on standard classification tasks. Furthermore, ASL's ability to adapt to various feature representations and classification tasks makes it a versatile solution. The code and pre-trained models for ASL are publicly available for further research and implementation. This work is the first to apply ASL to OSI, demonstrating its potential as a universal solution for this task. The authors also provide a comprehensive analysis of ASL's performance on benchmark datasets, highlighting its advantages and limitations. Time series data often exhibit complex patterns, and when dealing with numerous series, it can be difficult to identify meaningful trends. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach that combines dimension reduction and clustering of time series data. This method utilizes factor-adjusted vector autoregressive modelling to estimate the number of groups within the time series data and derive cluster-specific characteristics. Our approach is based on a two-stage process, where the first stage estimates factor models to identify common patterns across the time series data, and the second stage uses a vector autoregressive model to determine the number of clusters and their underlying structures. We have also derived theoretical limits for the performance of our method in high-dimensional time series data. Our approach is demonstrated through simulations and real-world applications involving macroeconomic data and social media time series. Furthermore, we have developed a software package in R to facilitate the implementation of our method for high-dimensional time series data analysis.
